entities.name: Saint Patrick's Cathedral
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
St Patrick's Cathedral in New York City, the largest decorated Gothic Revival Catholic church in the United States, completed in 1878 and designed by James Renwick Jr. on Fifth Avenue facing Rockefeller Center, served as the physical symbol of Irish Catholic immigrant identity in America — built when Irish immigrants were the most despised ethnic group in American cities, and now receiving 5.5 million visitors annually in New York's most expensive real estate district. The cathedral's construction (1858-1878) during the Civil War era represented an act of community assertion by a community facing 'No Irish Need Apply' discrimination.

Archbishop John Hughes ('Dagger John'), who commissioned the cathedral in 1858, was the most combative figure in American Catholic history — he had threatened to burn New York to the ground if Catholic churches were attacked during anti-Irish riots. The site on Fifth Avenue at 50th Street was then outside the city limits, with Archbishop Hughes purchasing it precisely because it was remote — he foresaw Manhattan's northward expansion. The cathedral cost $2 million, financed almost entirely by small donations from Irish immigrant workers.

St Patrick's Cathedral has hosted the funerals of every New York Cardinal, Robert F. Kennedy's 1968 funeral, Babe Ruth's funeral (1948), and the funerals of multiple NYPD and FDNY officers — becoming the ceremonial center of New York's Catholic institutional life. The cathedral's Lady Chapel (east end), choir and liturgical music program, and annual St Patrick's Day connections make it the most symbolically loaded Catholic building in America. The 2015 renovation ($175 million) restored it to its Victorian polychrome marble interior.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: St Patrick's Cathedral's construction by Irish immigrants facing systematic discrimination — and its transformation into the ceremonial center of American Catholic life hosting Kennedy funerals, presidential masses, and civic ceremonies — is the most complete architectural embodiment of immigrant community assertion in American history.
